title: Show HN: AWKLog – a minimalist Datalog interpreter in Awk
author: stass
content_excerpt:
For many of the projects I work on I found myself wanting to use a relational language like Datalog to generate C source from specifications, do verification during build or maintain a task database.

However pulling a full blown Souffle or SWI-PL as a build dependency is always a PITA and also an overkill.

So I (with the help of Claude) built awklog, a pure POSIX awk based interpreter. Copy it to your project and use during build stage or test stage with no extra dependencies.

It's a semi-naive interpreter, so decently fast, and certainly fast enough for anything you might need to do as a dev tool.

One cool usecase in particular I've been a heavy user of is a task system maintained directly in the project git repo. Just create a text file with tuples describing your tasks, their states, dependencies, hypotheses and so on. AWKLog will be able to query it for you, even recursively, and provide instant answers. Easy for AI agents to query too and no remote infrastructure dependencies at all. Everything stays in GIT, version controlled.

I hope other people will find this tool useful too.

title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
author: dataflow
content_excerpt:
> understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions

He phrases it like these criteria are requirements, but they really aren't for every problem. They make sense for those theoretical problems whose solutions' main values lie in their understandability and further development, but not every problem is like that. Some problems' solutions are just revolutionary on their own even if you contribute or understand absolutely nothing else. AI technology itself is an example of this!

To give a trivial hypothetical counterexample: if you came up with a solution for the traveling salesman problem that is both empirically sufficiently faster than the state of the art, that is an immense contribution and you absolutely deserve the credit for it regardless of whether you or anyone else understands how/why it works. It could literally even produce wrong results 50% of the time and still revolutionize humanity if it's efficient enough when it's correct. Denying them credit because they didn't understand the algorithm would be ludicrous - the results stand & speak for themselves.

Statisticians, traditional-AI researchers, etc. had to learn this the hard way when (basically black-box) neural nets became so good that their otherwise-elegant & explainable classical algorithms just stopped being able to compete in more and more applications, and got left behind. Are mathematicians looking to repeat that history?

title: AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System
author: bitwize
content_excerpt:
...For now.

Frontier models are generating sensible abstract engineering decisions for nontrivial code bases. Phase 1 (GPT 4 era) was "fancy autocomplete": it could generate a function or complete a clause before losing the plot. Phase 2 (Opus 4.x era) was the spec-driven development era, involving careful construction of guardrails and guidelines and steering the agents as they worked. Phase 3 is the beginning of the "software factory" era. You can now one-shot nontrivial apps with a prompt that leaves most of the specifics up to the agents. You just can't do this for like, a whole enterprise—maybe a microservice.

Another phase or two, and you can pretty much say goodbye to 95% of SWE jobs. The only people left involved in the software development process will be business analysts, product managers, and perhaps designers if they don't want the UI to look all "AI ass-ugly". A handful of trillion-dollar companies will retain a few really smart people who could code by hand if they wanted to, to keep the models trained and topped up on good practices. But line-of-business, which was the bread and butter for software engineers for going on 70 years now, will be done by machine. Humans will specify, and humans will QA the results, and that's it.

title: Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026)
author: srid68
content_excerpt:
1-year part-time experiment: can you build a large project with AI writing the code and AI plus deterministic tools verifying/guiding/enforcing it for structural and behavior consistency, without a human reading the code?

I'm building a polyglot web framework in 15 languages, with C# and Lean4 as the reference implementations. Structural and behavioral audits using deterministic tools check that every port stays consistent with the reference. It's about 1.8M lines now. I have not reviewed the code/neither have i verified the behavior tests except at the time of giving requirement and never seen some of the language code at all.

The question is how far can we produce "working code → correct code [Possible] → good code [Unknown]" with deterministic audits correcting structure, ai mistakes and behavior validation.

So far the quality looks acceptable with lots of correction of AI output done without looking, but it isn't fully verified.

Line counts per language, with changes since August: https://claude.ai/artifact/5f1m1pTM7tZ4boQzwsoAG7

I am still trying to work out what is it though, so well we will see when we get there.

author: lnkdinsuxs
content_excerpt:
> It's going to enable me to do less software development and more marketing? Goodie, I'm so happy I could puke.

If you hate marketing, don't do it. If you enjoy software development, have fun doing it.

However, you will remain an employee and you have to appreciate the pros and cons of being an employee. The other thing you have to appreciate is that the number of employees writing code who are AI, are cheaper than any human on the planet and works 24x7 without complaining or asking for a raise is going to go up. Likely exponentially.

This doesn't mean demand for good software developers is going to go down, but increasingly, software development is likely going to look like how one human Amazon warehouse worker wears special harnesses that allow them to lift far more weight, walk longer distances and interact with dozens of robots in the warehouse.

As I said in the parent it's not for everyone but a lot more people who were struggling to start their own venture will now be more capable of and have more freedom.

It might very well turn out that in a few years, the only way to enjoy software development the way you like it, is to establish your own boutique software development company.

title: Show HN: Nonce – Open-source, least-privilege Gmail access for AI agents
author: richardmeng
content_excerpt:
Hi HN! We built nonce, an open-source tool that sits between personal AI agents (Muse, Grok, ChatGPT, Claude) and your personal data in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and more.

Today, if you connect Gmail to an AI agent like Muse, it can read your entire inbox. Whether on purpose or not, they can read far more emails than needed. This poses a huge data-privilege risk, in which personal data is accessed without limits.

With nonce, the AI will no longer hold your Google or Slack tokens. To read anything, it has to show its intent first:

User's question: When does my flight to Tokyo leave? Agent's justification: Need the airline confirmation email Agent's search query: from:united.com Tokyo Access needed: 10 minutes

If the justification and search query are reasonable, nonce issues a scoped token to the AI Agent. AI Agent can only query data using a token.

If something looks fishy, i.e the AI is acting on its own, wants too much, or wants sensitive emails like bank statements, medical results, or password resets. nonce sends you a notification to approve or deny.

By default, nonce denies massive crawling behaviors

How it works 1. nonce scores each search against your original question before running it, to ensure its relevance. 2. Every search is combined with the token's search. If the AI searches "bank statement", nonce runs (from:united.com Tokyo) AND (bank statement). It can narrow its access, but not widen it. 3. The token is scoped to that agent only, with a TTL for X minutes.

title: Show HN: Doozy – an AI coworker in Slack that works in prod without your keys
author: shivsarthak
content_excerpt:
I built Doozy because support at my company (Spur) is understaffed and kept waiting on engineering to run a query for a customer, or to check whether something was a bug. The first version was a Slack bot with read access to our Postgres and Stripe, and it was very hacky. It could barely read files sent in a thread, but the agent was smart enough to find them through Slack search and finish the task anyway. It got used far more by support and success than by engineers, which surprised me. 13 people at Spur use it every day; it's basically a critical part of the team now.

Doozy is the rebuilt, multi-tenant version. You mention it in a thread with a task, it runs the task against your systems (database, Stripe, GitHub, Linear, PostHog, any MCP server, the web) in its own isolated environment, and posts the result and files in the thread.

How it touches production:

- Every job runs in a fresh sandbox (E2B today) with no credentials in it. Model calls, tool calls and git go through gateways outside the sandbox that add credentials per request. A prompt injection can make the agent misuse the tools it has, but it can't exfiltrate a key, because there isn't one to read. - Secrets the agent genuinely needs inside the sandbox (an SSH key, a CLI token) are handed over only when it asks for a named secret with a reason, and that request is logged. - Tools marked destructive start denied. Owners turn them on per tool. - Every external action writes a receipt in the thread and an append-only audit log.

title: Electrification Could Cut Global Energy Use in Half
author: jonhohle
content_excerpt:
Most people aren’t familiar with a peak demand rate because it’s not common in many markets. Take the highest kW use period of the month, and multiply kW demand by $20. Run the oven; pulls 3kW; $60. Run the oven and the stove top (1.8kW) at the same time $96. Screw up one time during the month and you might as well not care about the rest of the month.

I’m being a bit hyperbolic - it’s averaged over the highest 1 hour peak demand period (4pm-7pm, M-F), but it does limit what things can be run simultaneously (no dryer, oven and AC at the same time, for example). We schedule things around that, Our peak demand for this past month was 2.3kW. That single line item charge is higher than our entire gas bill.

There’s a separate use charge as well, but per kWh that’s pretty low. Then, of course, there’s the dozens of other random charges and fees ($86) that have nothing to do with electricity generation and everything to do with being a monopoly (court resolution surcharge: $3.58). The idea of moving more things to electric is nauseating.

title: Breaking the open web won't stop the bad bots
author: thaumasiotes
content_excerpt:
No, the definition of 'stealth bot' is a disaster. The proposed text criminalizes altering your user-agent string. It arguably criminalizes all existing user-agent strings, since their whole purpose is to lie about which browser you are.

Taking the first thing I could find, geekflare.com informs me that the current user-agent string for Google Chrome running on Windows 11 is

    Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/155.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
What's doing the work in the proposed text is the prohibition on using software "in a manner that is reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden the technical or commercial operation of" a service.

> Someone who is using a residential proxy network, headless browsing, and/or TLS fingerprint manipulation to evade rate limits and other controls to issue large volumes of automated requests under a deceptive UserAgent string isn't difficult to describe and differentiate versus a normal user using a UA.

Note that someone who's scripting a headless browser doesn't need to use a deceptive user-agent string. They can use the user-agent string for their browser, which isn't deceptive except to the degree that all user-agent strings are 90+% lies.
